capture.final_message:
Use the characterization of purely inseparable elements by Frobenius powers.

- First identify the perfect closure with the elements whose minimal polynomial has separable degree \(1\); this gives the first conjunct directly.

- For the right-hand universal statement, prove the standard equivalence
  \[
  \operatorname{natSepDegree}(\minpoly_F x)=1
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  x^{q^n}\in \operatorname{range}(F\to E)
  \text{ for some }n.
  \]
  The forward direction uses that an irreducible polynomial of separable degree \(1\) in characteristic exponent \(q\) is purely inseparable, hence becomes \(X^{q^n}-a\). Conversely, if \(x^{q^n}=a\in F\), then \(\minpoly_F(x)\) divides \(X^{q^n}-a\), so it has separable degree \(1\). If necessary, pass from the domain \(E\) to its fraction field to use the field-level formulation.

- For the left-hand universal statement, put
  \[
  K=F(S^q)\subseteq F(S).
  \]
  The inclusion \(K\subseteq F(S)\) is immediate. For each \(s\in S\), \(s^q\in K\), so \(s\) is purely inseparable over \(K\). But \(F(S)/F\), and therefore \(F(S)/K\), is separable by assumption. An element that is both separable and purely inseparable over \(K\) lies in \(K\); hence every \(s\in K\), giving \(F(S)=F(S^q)\).

Thus both universally quantified propositions follow from the same separable-versus-purely-inseparable mechanism, and the displayed `Iff` can be assembled by proving each side independently. The separability assumption on \(F(S)/F\) is essential: without it, adjoining \(q\)-th powers can genuinely produce a smaller field.
